## The Profile of the Bell Ringer: Trade, Vocation, and Oral Memory

In Almuñécar, there are just three men left who still climb the stone steps to the bell tower with the certainty of someone repeating a gesture learned in childhood. All three are retired, over seventy years old, and learned the trade between the fifties and the sixties, when manual ringing was not a heritage rarity, but the sonic pulse that ordered daily life. None appear on parish payrolls or municipal registers as professional bell ringers; such a position never formally existed in the town. Their bond with the bells was forged through family proximity, living near the tower, and a vocation that was then indistinguishable from simple availability.

The transmission of knowledge among the bell ringers of Almuñécar has followed a strictly oral pattern, similar to that documented by ethnographers in the Leonese regions where manual ringing retains a certain vitality. There, they describe a code of signals passed down from parents to children for generations, with local variants that function as dialects within a single language of bronze. In Almuñécar, this generational succession took place in the central decades of the twentieth century, when children accompanied their elders to the tower to hold the ropes, observe hand placement, and memorize the rhythmic sequences that distinguished a festive peal from a funeral toll. There was no written manual or formal school: learning was based on repetition, immediate correction, and the trust the veteran bell ringer placed in the apprentice, with a keen ear and patience.

The testimonies gathered from these three active bell ringers reveal that the trade was always linked to a social responsibility that transcended the merely technical. The bell ringer was neither a musician nor a laborer, but an intermediary between events and the community, someone capable of translating news into a sequence of strikes that all the neighbors knew how to interpret without need for explanation. This function demanded absolute availability: the bell ringer had to go to the tower at any hour of the day or night, in the middle of the harvest or during a storm, because the message allowed for no delays. The three men who keep the practice alive today in Almuñécar remember having interrupted meals, days of work in the fields, and family celebrations to answer an urgent call.

The oral memory preserved by these bell ringers is not limited to the technique of the ringing. Their accounts include anecdotes that illuminate the social meaning of each peal and the way the community responded to the coded messages. The alarm call, for example, was not an abstraction: it warned of fires in the nearby drylands or the presence of suspicious vessels off the coast, a distant echo of the Berber pirate attacks that ravaged the Granadan coastline for centuries. When the bell sounded with that urgent and staccato rhythm, the men abandoned their tasks and ran to the established meeting point, while the women secured the doors and gathered the children. The bell ringer who executed that call knew that the speed of the neighbors' response depended on the clarity of his ringing.

The funeral toll constitutes another fundamental chapter of that oral memory, and the bell ringers of Almuñécar describe it with a precision that reveals the complexity of the code. There was no single toll to announce a death, but variants that conveyed the age of the deceased and, consequently, the nature of the mourning. A child received a different toll than an adult, and that of an elderly person was in turn differentiated by a slower rhythm that the neighbors interpreted as the natural conclusion of a life cycle. This sonic gradation allowed the news to circulate through the town before anyone uttered a word, and prepared the community for the type of ceremony that was to be held.

The vocation of these bell ringers rests on a paradox that they themselves articulate without melodrama: they dedicate hours to a task that is no longer essential, in a time when electronic mechanisms can reproduce any peal with perfect regularity. However, their insistence on climbing the tower responds to a conviction that automation cannot replace. Manual ringing introduces variations imperceptible to an inattentive ear but significant to those who know the code: a slightly stronger strike, a pause an instant longer, an almost involuntary acceleration that betrays the bell ringer's emotion. This human texture of the sound constitutes, according to their own testimonies, the difference between informing and communicating.

The oral memory treasured by these three men also includes the names and peculiarities of the bells they have rung throughout their lives. Each has its own character, its response to the strike, its exact point where the clapper produces the cleanest sound. This knowledge does not appear in any inventory or heritage registry, and it will disappear with them if they do not find someone to pass it on to. The bell ringers know this, and that is why they insist on the urgency of a succession that is not forthcoming, a concern they share with the leaders of the local brotherhoods and which has become the focus of efforts to preserve the practice.

The profile of these retired bell ringers outlines a figure that no longer corresponds to any recognized trade in the labor market or in current ecclesiastical structures. They are, rather, custodians of a community knowledge that was transmitted orally for centuries and that today depends on the individual will of three people. Their authority does not stem from a title or an official appointment, but from the tacit recognition of the neighbors who still identify their names with the Torre de la Encarnación and with the sounds that have marked the decisive hours of local life. That silent legitimacy, built over decades, constitutes the ultimate foundation of a trade that resists disappearing as long as there are hands willing to pull the ropes.
